analysis.one_liner: Bans federal and state rules requiring handguns to have loaded-chamber indicators, magazine safeties, or microstamping.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late August 2024 with 13 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit any federal, state, or local government from requiring handguns sold in interstate commerce to include three safety features: a device showing whether the gun is loaded, a mechanism that prevents firing unless the magazine is fully inserted, and microstamping, which imprints a gun's identifying information on fired shell casings [S2]. It would also bar requirements for any technology that performs those functions or could be readily converted to do so, overriding stricter state handgun rules [S2]. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Handgun manufacturers and sellers, who would avoid the cost and complexity of adding chamber-loaded indicators, magazine safeties, or microstamping capability to comply with state rules; and handgun owners in states with stricter requirements, who could keep buying guns without those features [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids any government agency from requiring handguns to incorporate a device indicating whether the gun is loaded, or a mechanism preventing firing when the magazine is not fully inserted [S2].
It forbids requirements that handguns microstamp fired shell casings with the gun's make, model, and serial number, and blocks rules covering any related or convertible technology [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of the public in states that chose to require these safety features, who would lose loaded-chamber indicators, magazine safeties, and microstamping as protections; law enforcement would also lose microstamping, a tool that ties fired casings found at crime scenes to specific guns [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents of states with stricter gun rules

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state handgun safety rules, including California's microstamping requirement, which is designed to let investigators match shell casings found at crime scenes to the specific gun that fired them [S2].

Removing the magazine-safety requirement would allow handguns that can still fire when the magazine is removed, a feature safety advocates link to unintentional shootings by people who believe an unloaded gun is safe; the bill bars any rule requiring this safeguard [S2].
Supporters of the bill argue the required technologies are absent from firearms in common use and would raise costs for buyers and manufacturers, a cost an honest backer would acknowledge [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill lowers compliance costs for gun makers and spares buyers in strict states from feature mandates, but the trade is that residents of states that wanted these safeguards lose them, and investigators lose a forensic tool for matching casings to guns. The public-safety cost falls on the same general public the feature requirements were written for.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa introduced the bill on August 20, 2024, with nine original cosponsors [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
Thirteen Republicans served as cosponsors; no Democrat is listed [S3].
No further action was recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State regulators and existing state handgun safety rules, which remain in force because the bill never advanced; handgun buyers are left exactly where they were.

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action; the bill never received a hearing or a vote

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat appears in the record as a supporter, and no recorded opposition beyond the committee's inaction.

industries.note: The bill would spare manufacturers from having to add chamber-loaded indicators, magazine safeties, or microstamping capability to meet state rules [S2]. The savings come at the expense of the safety features and forensic traceability those rules were written to provide the public.
Retailers selling in strict states could continue stocking standard handguns without carrying feature-compliant models, though they face no direct obligation in the bill text [S2].
